name: ruzstd (pure-Rust zstd)
baseline: The zstd crate's bindings to the C reference zstd library
verdict_reason: No pure-Rust zstd beats the C bindings. ruzstd's own README puts its decoder 1.4x to 3.5x slower, its encoder lacks the default level, and Trifecta's newer libzstd-rs-sys port is about 3% slower than C by default.
tier_reason: First-party measurements taken with the time utility, with no hardware or compiler stated.
claimed_speedup: None: decoder about 3.5 times slower than C zstd on enwik9 and about 1.4 times slower on less compressible data; libzstd-rs-sys decompression a few percent (~3%) slower than C by default.
workload: Decoding enwik9.zst and an Ubuntu ISO compressed with zstd, from a ramfs.
platforms: Any Rust target (pure Rust, no C toolchain)
one_liner: Pure-Rust zstd decoder and partial encoder; 1.4x to 3.5x slower than the C library behind the zstd crate.
how_it_is_fast: It is not faster. It is a clean-room Rust implementation of RFC 8878 without the C library's hand-tuned decoding loops; its value is portability and no C toolchain.
use_it_when: You need zstd decoding on wasm, no_std or targets without a C toolchain and can accept slower decoding
skip_it_when: Speed matters: use the zstd crate (C bindings)
You need compression levels beyond Fastest; Default and higher are not implemented
caveats: The README's speed figures date from 2019 and were not rerun for later releases
Single-run time measurements with no hardware named
tradeoffs: Encoder supports only uncompressed and Fastest (about level 1) blocks
libzstd-rs-sys can match C only with an unsafe-performance-experimental flag that drops four bounds checks

evidence.quote: In terms of speed, `ruzstd` is behind the original C implementation
decoding the same enwik9.zst file from a ramfs
my decoder is about 3.5 times slower.
my decoder comes close to only being 1.4 times slower.
It also provides a compressor which is usable, but it does not yet reach the speed, ratio or configurability of the original zstd library.
By default decompression performance of our implementation is a few percent slower than the C reference implementation.
For most users a ~3% performance regression is likely an acceptable price to pay for increased memory safety.
